article_lead.description: a binary response probability to a normal score so a linear predictor yields valid fitted probabilities

new_bank_questions.title: Interpret a fitted probit dose curve
new_bank_questions.body: A binary probit model is p(x)=Φ(-1+0.5x). Find p at x=0, 2 and 4, the dose where p=0.5, and the local probability derivative at that dose. Explain why the coefficient is not a probability increase.
new_bank_questions.answer: The normal scores are -1, 0 and 1, giving p≈0.15866, 0.5 and 0.84134. The half-probability dose is x=2. The derivative there is 0.5φ(0)=0.5/√(2π)≈0.19947 per unit of x; elsewhere the derivative is 0.5φ(-1+0.5x), so it is not constant.

shared_changes.description: In the Probit link definition around line 783, qualify the statement that fitted probit coefficients are smaller than logit coefficients by a factor of about 1.6–1.8. It is an approximate comparison under comparable fitted curves, not an identity for any binary dataset or every coefficient. Check Probit link and dependent GLM/link pages.

In 'Three links' around lines 339–341, qualify the blanket claims that fitted logit and probit curves almost always agree and that goodness of fit will not motivate a switch. Their tails differ and model comparison depends on data and purpose. Check Introduction to GLMs, Probit link, Logit link and all linked comparison pages.
